attachments.origin_landmark: xiphoid process, costal cartilages 7-12 (bilateral), lumbar vertebrae L1-L3 via the crura, medial and lateral arcuate ligaments
attachments.insertion_landmark: central tendon (trefoil-shaped aponeurosis, midline; a single bone is named because the schema takes one insertion)

actions: primary muscle of inspiration (dome descends, increasing thoracic volume)

functional_compartments.name: Costal part
functional_compartments.function_note: Broadest part, arising from the costal margin's inner surface and running to the central tendon; the main contributor to dome descent (diaphragmatic breathing).
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

functional_compartments.name: Crural part
functional_compartments.function_note: Right crus (longer, arising from L1-L3) and left crus (from L1-L2) form the esophageal hiatus between them; the crural fibers surrounding the esophagus contribute an auxiliary sphincter-like action augmenting the lower esophageal sphincter -- a well-documented functional detail distinct from the costal part's pure ventilatory role.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

functional_compartments.name: Sternal part
functional_compartments.function_note: Smallest part, two small slips from the posterior xiphoid process; the sternocostal triangle gap between this and the costal part (foramen of Morgagni) is a recognized potential hernia site.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Two distinct real ultrasound-guided techniques are documented for this muscle, targeting different things. (1) Phrenic nerve block (the actual injection): linear probe transverse on the lateral neck at approximately the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6), lateral to the sternocleidomastoid; the nerve is identified as a small hypoechoic structure running obliquely on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle, deep to the prevertebral fascia. (2) Diagnostic diaphragm ultrasound (not an injection, but the standard real-time technique for confirming this muscle's location/function before or after any phrenic/intercostal block): linear probe in the 8th-9th intercostal space at the mid-to-anterior axillary line for the 'zone of apposition' thickness view, or a curvilinear/phased probe subcostally in the mid-clavicular line (right side via the liver acoustic window, left via the spleen) with M-mode for excursion.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: For the phrenic nerve block: the nerve lies superficial to the anterior scalene muscle belly, deep to sternocleidomastoid, medial to the brachial plexus trunks which run in the same interscalene groove more laterally/inferiorly. For diaphragm ultrasound at the zone of apposition: the muscle is seen as a distinct hyperechoic layer between the two hypoechoic peritoneal/pleural boundary lines in the lateral chest wall, thickening on inspiration.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Phrenic nerve block: a nerve stimulator confirming diaphragmatic twitch (hiccup-like contraction) without brachial plexus motor response is used to distinguish the phrenic nerve from the adjacent plexus trunks. Diaphragm ultrasound: at the zone of apposition the muscle is bounded by two bright lines (pleural line above, peritoneal line below) and visibly thickens with inspiration; from the subcostal window the muscle is seen as a curved bright line moving toward the probe on inspiration.
structures_at_risk: brachial plexus (adjacent trunks in the same interscalene fascial plane) -- inadvertent brachial plexus block/paresthesia if the injection is placed too far laterally or deep
vertebral artery, deep to the anterior scalene, at risk if the needle is advanced too deep
carotid artery and internal jugular vein, medial to the injection site

contralateral phrenic nerve function / respiratory compromise -- diaphragmatic paralysis is the intended local effect of a phrenic nerve block, which is exactly why it is used cautiously (e.g. as a diagnostic test before diaphragm plication) and never performed bilaterally
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: No motor-point/neural-arborization mapping specific to intramuscular BoNT injection into the diaphragm itself was found in the literature searched (unlike limb muscles, the diaphragm is not a BoNT-for-spasticity target in this atlas's clinical scope). What is well documented and genuinely useful here are (1) the ultrasound-guided phrenic nerve block, used diagnostically (e.g. to predict tolerance of diaphragmatic paralysis before plication surgery, or as an interscalene-block side-effect model) and therapeutically (intractable hiccups), and (2) diaphragm ultrasound itself as the standard real-time technique for assessing this muscle's thickness, thickening fraction, and excursion in ICU/perioperative practice -- included together because both are the real clinical 'injection/imaging approach' relevant to this muscle and its nerve.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Kang SS et al (2009) 'Unilateral phrenic nerve block guided by ultrasonography and nerve stimulator for the treatment of hiccup developed after tongue cancer operation: A case report', Korean J Anesthesiol 56(2):208-210, doi:10.4097/kjae.2009.56.2.208; Matamis D et al (2013) 'Sonographic evaluation of the diaphragm in critically ill patients. Technique and clinical applications', Intensive Care Med 39(5):801-810, doi:10.1007/s00134-013-2823-1 -- review of diaphragm ultrasound technique (zone-of-apposition thickness/thickening-fraction and subcostal excursion methods)
